title: Manual Handling: Lifting Safely
whatItIs: Manual handling means moving or supporting a load by hand or bodily force: lifting, putting down, pushing, pulling or carrying. It is a major cause of back and joint injuries on site.

keyFacts.text: Employers MUST avoid manual handling that risks injury, so far as is reasonably practicable.
If it can't be avoided, employers MUST assess it and reduce the risk to the lowest level reasonably practicable.
Where reasonably practicable, employers MUST say how heavy each load is and which side is heaviest.
Employees MUST make full and proper use of the safe system of work provided for handling.

keyFacts: The law sets no 'safe' weight limit. Risk depends on the load, the task, how often, and the conditions.
One bad lift can cause a lifetime of pain, but most injuries build up from repeated handling.

visual.caption: The legal order: avoid, assess, reduce

items.title: Avoid
items.text: Don't move it, deliver to point of use, or use a hoist, telehandler or pallet truck.

items.title: Assess
items.text: Look at the task, the load, the working environment and the person doing it.

items.title: Reduce
items.text: Lighter or smaller loads, handling aids, better layout, team lifts planned with care.

items.title: Train
items.text: Good handling technique adds to these controls. It never replaces them.

a.label: Lifting technique training
points: A useful extra once the risk has been reduced
Can't make up for bad tasks, unsuitable loads or no lifting aids

b.label: Avoiding or mechanising the lift
points: The first step the law requires
e.g. hoists, conveyors, materials delivered to where they're used

onTheTest.question: Under the Manual Handling Operations Regulations, what must an employer try to do first?
options: Avoid hazardous manual handling where reasonably practicable
Set a 25 kg limit for every load
Make workers sign a lifting declaration
onTheTest.why: Regulation 4: avoid hazardous manual handling so far as reasonably practicable; if it can't be avoided, assess it and reduce the risk.

onTheTest.question: Two workers are going to share a heavy, awkward load. Which of these increases the risk?
options: They plan the lift before starting
They are very different in size and strength
They've been trained in team lifts
onTheTest.why: HSG150: plan shared lifts carefully. Hazards arise when people are not equally matched in size and strength, or not trained in team lifts.

traps: There's no legal 'safe' weight: even a light load can injure if handled badly or too often.
Training alone won't make a badly designed task safe: avoid or mechanise first.
Pushing and pulling are manual handling too, not just lifting.
Hurt your back? Get early medical advice and return to heavy handling gradually.
